title: Section check: Buildings, belief and shared places
intro: 10 questions about Lessons 6–10. Take your time. You can look back at the lessons and try again as often as you like.

questions.question: The posts and beams of a tongkonan are part of its structure. What does structure mean?

options.text: The parts that hold a building up
options.feedback: Yes. The structure is the parts that hold a building up, and how they fit together.

options.text: The carved designs on the front walls
options.feedback: Not quite. Carved designs are ornament. The structure is the posts and frame that hold the house up. Look back at Lesson 6.

options.text: The open space where people meet
options.feedback: Not quite. The open space is between the buildings. The structure holds a building up. Look back at Lesson 6.

questions.question: Look at the two photos of Toraja houses. Which question can they help you answer?

options.text: Who lived in each room of the house?
options.feedback: Not quite. The photos show the outside. They do not show who lived in each room. Look back at Lesson 6.

options.text: What do all Toraja people believe today?
options.feedback: Not quite. A photo of a building cannot show what a whole community believes. Look back at Lesson 6.

options.text: What shape are the roofs and posts?
options.feedback: Yes. We can see the roofs, posts and repeated shapes. We can also see how the houses stand together.

questions.question: Borobudur's walls have many reliefs. What is a relief?

options.text: A long walkway that goes around a building
options.feedback: Not quite. A long walkway is a gallery. The reliefs are the carvings on its walls. Look back at Lesson 7.

options.text: A carving that stands out from a wall
options.feedback: Yes. A relief stands out from a flat background. At Borobudur, reliefs tell stories in stone.

options.text: A journey to a place that is holy
options.feedback: Not quite. A journey to a holy place is a pilgrimage. A relief is a kind of carving. Look back at Lesson 7.

questions.question: How did Borobudur's design guide the way people moved through it?

options.text: People walked past carved stories, then climbed up.
options.feedback: Yes. People walked around the galleries past the reliefs. Then they climbed towards the top terraces.

options.text: People stayed in one dark room in the middle.
options.feedback: Not quite. Borobudur has terraces and walkways that rise to the top. People moved through it. Look back at Lesson 7.

options.text: People only looked at it from far across the valley.
options.feedback: Not quite. People walked around its galleries and climbed its levels. Look back at Lesson 7.

questions.question: The lesson says Angkor Wat's moat did not need to have only one purpose. Why?

options.text: It was dug long after the temple.
options.feedback: Not quite. The moat is part of the temple's plan. It helps make the temple a picture of a universe. Look back at Lesson 8.

options.text: It was only there to make it look pretty.
options.feedback: Not quite. The moat had meaning, and the land around it had water works for farming. Look back at Lesson 8.

options.text: It could be sacred and useful too.
options.feedback: Yes. The moat helped show a sacred universe. It also sat in a landscape of canals and water works.

questions.question: Words carved at Angkor Wat from the 1500s to the 1700s tell of pilgrims' visits. What do they show?

options.text: The temple was first built in the 1500s.
options.feedback: Not quite. Angkor Wat was built in the 1100s. The carved words came much later. Look back at Lesson 8.

options.text: Later people gave the temple new meaning.
options.feedback: Yes. The temple became a Buddhist holy place. Pilgrims, some of them royal, came to pray there.

options.text: Every part changed religion on one date.
options.feedback: Not quite. The change was a long process. It did not happen on one single date. Look back at Lesson 8.

questions.question: What does an airwell do in a long shophouse?

options.text: It shelters people walking past.
options.feedback: Not quite. That is the five-foot way, a covered path along the front. Look back at Lesson 9.

options.text: It brings in light and fresh air.
options.feedback: Yes. An airwell is an open space inside. It brings light and air into deep rooms.

options.text: It stores water for the shop below.
options.feedback: Not quite. An airwell is an open space that lets in light and fresh air. Look back at Lesson 9.

stimulus.title: A made-up photo of a made-up port
stimulus.body: This is a made-up example. A photo shows a row of grand houses beside a canal in the made-up port of Velmar. The houses are tall and made of brick. Their fronts are clean and decorated.

questions.question: Which question would need other sources, such as city records?

options.text: How was each house paid for?
options.feedback: Yes. A street view cannot show where the money came from. Records can tell us more.

options.text: What are the houses made of?
options.feedback: Not quite. You can see in the photo that the houses are brick. Look back at Lesson 9.

options.text: Do the houses stand by a canal?
options.feedback: Not quite. The photo shows the canal. You need records for what a photo cannot show. Look back at Lesson 9.

questions.question: In Ifugao, each family owns its own fields. Why do families also work as a team?

options.text: Every field belongs to the whole village.
options.feedback: Not quite. Each household owns its own terraces. Shared work does not mean shared fields. Look back at Lesson 10.

options.text: Only one family knows how to grow rice.
options.feedback: Not quite. Many people pass on knowledge about seeds, soil and water. Look back at Lesson 10.

options.text: Walls and water need shared care.
options.feedback: Yes. Walls and water systems link the fields. So each household depends on its neighbours.

stimulus.title: A made-up valley
stimulus.body: This is a made-up example. In the made-up valley of Orun, farmers grow rice on terraces. A small wood grows above the terraces. One year, people cut down most of the trees. After that, the water reaching the fields was hard to control.

questions.question: Which idea from Lesson 10 helps explain what happened in Orun?

options.text: Woods above terraces help control water.
options.feedback: Yes. Small woods above the terraces help control the water that reaches the fields.

options.text: Terraces need no care once they are built.
options.feedback: Not quite. Fields, walls and water need care all the time. Look back at Lesson 10.

options.text: A terrace is only a pretty pattern on a hill.
options.feedback: Not quite. Terraces are farming work. Land, walls, water and woods are all linked. Look back at Lesson 10.

results.high: Well done. You know a lot about how buildings and places shape people's lives.
results.middle: Good work. You remember many of the main ideas. Look back at any lesson you want to check.
results.low: Thank you for trying. Look back at Lessons 6–10, then try again whenever you like.
